If your Divvy (BILL Spend & Expense) card program has stopped fitting how you pay, you're probably comparing Divvy alternatives. Divvy here means the corporate card and expense software, as opposed to Chicago's bike share or the window-manager app. BILL[completed its acquisition of Divvy](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1786352/000119312521178541/d189628dex991.htm) on June 1, 2021, and the product now ships as BILL Spend & Expense with the BILL Divvy Card.


Price is unlikely to be the trigger, because BILL lists the software with no per-user fee. The reasons to leave are mechanical. The card must be paid every cycle, rewards shrink when you pay monthly, and vendor payments often run through a separate system.


Each Divvy alternative handles those problems differently. The[spend management](https://www.corpay.com/resources/blog/what-is-spend-management) market has split into card-first platforms, HR-led suites, and services that run AP for you.


## Key takeaways


-


Divvy is a charge card, so the balance is due every cycle, and its rewards multipliers rise the more often you pay.


-


BILL lists Spend & Expense with no per-user software fee, while BILL's bill pay is a separate subscription priced per user.


-


Ramp and Brex include bill pay in their free tiers, Navan Expense leans toward travel, and Rippling Spend ties spend to HR.


-


If vendor payments outweigh employee card spend, judge each option on how it pays vendors before comparing card features.


-


Check the credit line, rewards rules, entities, ERP sync, and data export before you switch.

## What is Divvy, and why do teams look for alternatives?


Divvy is BILL's corporate charge card and expense software, now sold as BILL Spend & Expense. BILL lists the software with no per-user fee, so teams that leave usually cite card structure, rewards rules, or AP fit.


Divvy earns its place on most shortlists. BILL lists credit lines from $1,000 up to $5M, with no annual fees or interest charges. One credit application covers all of a company's entities, and Divvy expense management and reimbursements come included. BILL names two-way syncs with QuickBooks, Oracle NetSuite, Xero, Sage Intacct, and Acumatica. Applicants need a US business bank account and an EIN.


Card structure is where fit gets tested. People search for a "Divvy business credit card," but BILL calls the BILL Divvy Card a corporate charge card, due in full each cycle.[Regulation Z defines a charge card](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1026/2/) as one where "no periodic rate is used to compute a finance charge."


That rule is written for consumer accounts, but the mechanism carries over. With no revolving option, every statement is a cash event your forecast has to absorb. There's a longer breakdown of how a[charge card and a credit card](https://www.corpay.com/resources/blog/charge-card-vs-credit-card) differ for business use.


### Is Divvy still free?


The software is, according to BILL's pricing page, which lists Spend & Expense with no per-user software fee. Card fees can still apply, such as late or returned payment and foreign currency fees.


The bigger cost question is AP. BILL's AP and AR plans are paid subscriptions priced per user, and ACH and check payments carry per-payment fees. A team paying hundreds of vendor invoices a month through BILL is buying two products with two pricing models. Free software also raises a fair question about who pays for it.


### How do Divvy rewards change with payment frequency?


Divvy rewards multipliers rise as you pay more often. BILL's rewards page sets the highest multipliers for weekly, daily, or prepaid accounts.


Take a month with $4,000 of "everything else" spend and $1,000 at restaurants. Paid weekly, the $4,000 earns 6,000 points and the restaurant spend earns 7,000. Paid monthly, the same spend earns 4,000 and 2,000 points.


Multipliers apply to the first $5,000 spent in a month, and foreign transactions earn no points. The rule that's easy to miss is retention. To keep a month's rewards, BILL says "you must spend at least 30% of your credit line."


On a $100,000 line, you must spend $30,000 that month to retain your points, even though multipliers stop at $5,000. A generous line can cost you a month's points in a slow quarter.


Whether weekly payment is worth it depends on your cash-forecast discipline. If you already forecast weekly, the extra points may cost little added work. If cash runs tight around payroll, weekly debits add strain that points may or may not offset. I don't think there's a general answer.

In a Ramp vs. Divvy decision, the sharpest difference is bill pay, which Ramp includes in its free tier. In a Brex vs. Divvy comparison, card structure comes first, since Brex's disclosures describe a credit card. For tools beyond these six, see this review of[expense management software](https://www.corpay.com/resources/blog/best-expense-management-software) .


### Which alternatives charge per user?


Most do in some form. Ramp and Brex pair a free tier with a paid per-user tier and custom Enterprise pricing. Navan Expense is free for a small number of monthly users, then priced per user, and Rippling quotes Spend by request.


Per-user pricing scales with cardholders, and total spend doesn't enter the formula. A 200-person field crew with a card per technician pays far more in seat fees than a 20-person office with the same spend. Count your likely cardholders in year two, since multi-entity support and deeper ERP syncs sit in paid tiers.


### Which alternatives include accounts payable?


Ramp and Brex include bill pay in their free tiers. Rippling sells bill pay as a separate product, BILL's AP is a separate paid plan, and Navan's expense pages don't address bill pay either way.


"Includes bill pay" and "manages vendor payments" describe different jobs. Bill pay software sends the payment you approve. A managed service also enrolls vendors, keeps their banking details current, and chases exceptions when a payment bounces. If your AP team spends its week on vendor calls, ask every finalist who answers them.


## Which Divvy alternative fits which company?


The right Divvy alternative depends less on features than on where your spend goes, whether that's employee cards, travel, or vendor payments. Match the platform to the largest of the three.


Two fits are simple. Staying on BILL makes sense if AP volume is light and your team already works in BILL daily. Rippling Spend fits companies already running HR and payroll on Rippling, since Spend adds cards, expenses, bills, travel, and procurement.


### Best for funded startups


Ramp and Brex are the usual picks for venture-backed teams that want cards, expenses, and bill pay without a software bill on day one. Ramp's card is a corporate liability charge card with 30-day payback, and Brex describes its card as a corporate credit card.


Entity limits matter less at the first acquisition than the second. On Brex Essentials, a parent and one subsidiary fit the two-entity limit, but a third entity means moving up a tier. On Ramp, any second entity means Plus, so price the upgrade before you sign.


### Best for travel-heavy teams


Navan Expense suits teams whose biggest spend problem is travel. Booking is included, the Navan card offers up to 1.5% back, and you can link existing Visa, Mastercard, or Amex cards instead.


When travel drives the spend, booking policy is the control that counts. A merchant restriction can't stop a rep from booking a pricey fare three days out. Ask how out-of-policy bookings route for approval before the ticket is issued.


### Best for companies paying many vendors


If most of your outflow goes to vendors, the card is the smaller decision. Nacha reports close to 8.1 billion[B2B payments on the ACH Network](https://www.nacha.org/news/same-day-ach-and-business-business-payments-propel-ach-network-volume-growth-2025) in 2025, with B2B volume up almost 10%.


Checks haven't disappeared either. In AFP's Digital Payments Survey, as reported by Nacha, 81% of B2B payments involved paper checks in 2004. The 2025 edition still shows checks at[26% of B2B payments](https://www.nacha.org/news/over-21-years-massive-drop-b2b-check-payments-study-finds) .


A card platform that ignores those rails leaves much of your payables in a separate system. Corpay fits this profile, pairing commercial cards with fully managed AP that pays vendors by virtual card, ACH, or check. Corpay's team handles vendor data, payment execution, and error resolution, so vendor follow-up moves off your AP clerk's desk.

## What should you check before switching from Divvy?


Before you switch from Divvy, check seven things, which are credit line, rewards rules, entities, ERP sync, AP coverage, fraud controls, and data export.


1.


Ask whether the card is charge or credit, what the payback period is, and what happens to your line after a slow quarter.


2.


Compare rewards with rebates, and ask each vendor how its program makes money if the software is free.


3.


Count your entities today and two years out, then check each tier's entity limit against that number.


4.


Request field-level ERP mapping for class, location, and department, and confirm which ERPs sit on which tier.


5.


Decide whether you need card-only spend,[bill pay software](https://www.corpay.com/resources/blog/accounts-payable-management-software) , or a service that manages vendor payments for you.


6.


Check for single-use virtual cards, merchant locks, and real-time alerts, and ask how card fraud disputes are handled.


7.


Plan the card cutover, reissue dates, and the export of historical transactions and receipts before the old account closes.


On the first item, payback period is the cash question that matters most, and this primer on[how company credit cards work](https://www.corpay.com/resources/blog/how-company-credit-cards-work) frames it.


The second item comes down to interchange, a fee paid between banks on each card purchase.[Visa's US interchange schedule](https://usa.visa.com/content/dam/VCOM/download/merchants/visa-usa-interchange-reimbursement-fees.pdf) , dated Oct. 24, 2026, lists 2.70% + $0.10 for commercial card-not-present transactions in its Purchasing & Corporate T&E column.[CFPB research on card rewards](https://files.consumerfinance.gov/f/documents/cfpb_credit-card-rewards_issue-spotlight_2024-05.pdf) adds that issuers may also fund rewards through annual fees or merchant-funded offers.


None of that tells you how a specific vendor funds its program, so ask, and ask what changes if your volume drops.


The sixth item deserves weight because risk sits unevenly across payment types. According to AFP's[2026 Payments Fraud and Control Survey](https://www.truist.com/content/dam/truist-bank/us/en/documents/info/cci/2026-afp-payments-fraud-control-survey-report-key-highlights.pdf) , 58% of organizations reported attempted or actual check fraud in 2025. The figure for corporate/commercial credit cards was 21% of organizations.


Those are shares of organizations reporting attempted or actual fraud, which isn't a fraud rate. Most respondents work at companies with $1 billion or more in revenue. The numbers still support pairing cards with[card controls and spend policies](https://www.corpay.com/resources/blog/card-controls-spend-policies) that block merchants you never buy from.


On the last item, ask for a test export of last quarter's transactions, with receipts attached, during the demo and before you sign. If the vendor can't produce it, expect the same friction when you leave. Run the same test on your Divvy account, because your audit records have to come out before it closes.


Each check maps to cash, control, or close time. Payback period and line size set your cash rhythm, while entity limits and fraud controls set your control. ERP mapping and AP coverage decide how much manual coding lands on your team at month end.
